title: Composite Actions
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of composite actions and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to composite actions.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on composite actions. A composite action groups several steps behind `action.yml` metadata and a stable set of documented inputs and outputs. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Composite Actions matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: A composite action groups several steps behind `action.yml` metadata and a stable set of documented inputs and outputs. Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: What a composite action is
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Defining inputs and outputs
items.text: Write one step output as `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then declare job outputs if a downstream job needs the value. Use `$GITHUB_ENV` for values needed by later steps in the same job.

items.title: Combining multiple steps
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Passing shell and environment configuration
items.text: Use a GitHub Environment for deployment-specific secrets, variables, branch restrictions, and reviewer gates. Do not treat an environment name alone as proof that approval rules are configured.

items.title: When composite actions are appropriate
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

content_blocks.code:
# action.yml
name: Repository checks
description: Run shared, non-destructive checks
inputs:
  message:
    description: Status message
    required: false
    default: "Checks ready"
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Print status
      shell: bash
      env:
        MESSAGE: ${{ inputs.message }}
      run: echo "$MESSAGE"
content_blocks.expected_output: A composite action exposes a `message` input and executes one shell step. Inputs are passed through an environment variable.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Place `action.yml` in an action directory and call it with `uses: ./path/to/action`. Test empty, normal, and unexpected input values.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original snippet and remove temporary workflow changes. If you triggered a real run, inspect the run log before editing the file again.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to composite actions. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain composite actions, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Package shared workflow logic behind clear input/output contracts and maintained versions.

content.task: Apply composite actions to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: A composite action groups several steps behind `action.yml` metadata and a stable set of documented inputs and outputs.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: A composite action groups several steps behind `action.yml` metadata and a stable set of documented inputs and outputs. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
